section_summary: This section consists chiefly of FCC Radio Intelligence Division copies of Dōmei press broadcasts intercepted in July and August 1943, together with two confidential FCC forwarding letters to Assistant Secretary of State Adolf A. Berle Jr. The broadcasts combine news, military claims, economic-mobilization reports, and Axis propaganda concerning the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere, Philippine and Burmese independence, the bombing of Rome, Japanese operations across Asia and the Pacific, and Allied policy toward neutral states. Several transmissions are in Japanese or French, while substantial portions consist only of encrypted numerical groups or fragmentary, unreadable text.

subfiles.title: Continuation of Dōmei press intercept: Laurel, Bose, the Vatican, and Thailand
subfiles.to: General radio audience; intercepted by U.S. monitoring personnel
subfiles.about: Continuation of a multipart Dōmei broadcast reporting on Philippine constitutional preparations, the Pope, Subhas Chandra Bose, and Thai territorial negotiations.
subfiles.summary: The Philippine item describes José P. Laurel's work with the Independence Preparatory Commission after meeting Prime Minister Tojo in Manila. Other items report speculation that Pope Pius XII might leave Vatican City during further raids on Rome, reproduce Bose's address to graduating Indian National Army officers at Shōnan, and note Thai preparations for negotiations with the Japanese embassy.

subfiles.title: Japanese-language Dōmei intercept on Bose and the fighting at Munda
subfiles.to: General radio audience; intercepted by U.S. monitoring personnel
subfiles.about: Japanese-language reports cover an Indian officer graduation at Shōnan and Japanese propaganda about American operations around Munda.
subfiles.summary: The first report describes Subhas Chandra Bose exhorting new Indian National Army officers to fight for independence. A much longer item, attributed to reporting from Lisbon and London, portrays American troops near Munda as stalled by Japanese jungle defenses and suffering heavy physical and psychological strain.

subfiles.title: Four-page Japanese Dōmei press intercept
subfiles.to: FCC monitoring station at Honolulu
subfiles.about: A four-page Japanese-language broadcast reports on Japanese economic relations with China, Ba Maw's meetings, shipping consolidation, and domestic administrative mobilization.
subfiles.summary: Masatsune Ogura discusses the Japanese economic mission to China, trade, prices, and the need for closer planned economic cooperation. Ba Maw reports favorable talks with Tojo and Bose about Burmese independence and assistance to India's independence movement; later items concern shipping-company consolidation and Tojo's instructions to regional administrators on production, food, and wartime government.

subfiles.title: French-language Dōmei intercept on Burma, regional administration, Rome, and Indochina
subfiles.to: General radio audience; intercepted by the FCC
subfiles.about: French-language Dōmei items discuss a Burmese association, Manchukuo officials, Japanese regional administration, Indian nationalists, the bombing of Rome, and a French appointment in Indochina.
subfiles.summary: The broadcast announces a new Burmese association in Tokyo, reports Cheng Yu's return from Thailand, and describes a conference of Japanese regional administrative councils chaired in Tojo's presence. It also covers Indian delegates traveling to meet Bose, changes affecting Thai residents in French Indochina, an Asahi denunciation of the Allied bombing of Rome, and Captain Robin's appointment to a Franco-Japanese relations post.

subfiles.title: Dōmei intercept on culture, air raids, medicine, Filipino students, and physical training
subfiles.to: General radio audience; intercepted by the FCC
subfiles.about: A multipart English broadcast reports a cultural-script contest, Japanese naval raids, ipecac cultivation, Filipino students in Japan, a German decoration, and a national fitness campaign.
subfiles.summary: The items announce a Board of Information dramatic-writing contest and claim successful Japanese attacks on Ceylon, Kanton Island, and Vanikoro. Other reports promote large-scale Malayan cultivation of ipecac, describe Filipino students visiting Japanese ministries, report Hitler's decoration of Kanagawa governor Jōtarō Kondō, and outline a month-long physical and military-training movement.

subfiles.title: Dōmei intercept on Pacific operations, co-prosperity construction, Singapore salvage, and Rome
subfiles.to: General radio audience; intercepted by the FCC
subfiles.about: English Dōmei items present Japanese military claims and propaganda about economic construction, the Singapore dry dock, and the bombing of Rome.
subfiles.summary: The broadcast repeats claims of air attacks on Ceylon, Kanton, Vanikoro, and Allied aircraft near Buin, then praises Japanese-sponsored industrial development in Burma and the Philippines as evidence of the Co-Prosperity Sphere. It also reports Captain Robin's appointment, the refloating of the King George V dry dock at Seletar, and Tomokazu Hori's denunciation of Anglo-American bombing damage to Rome's San Lorenzo Basilica and Campo Verano.

subfiles.title: Japanese Dōmei intercept on railway production and the Chinese Communist crisis
subfiles.to: General radio audience; intercepted by U.S. monitoring personnel
subfiles.about: A Japanese-language broadcast describes centralized railway rolling-stock production and comments on tensions between Chiang Kai-shek's government and the Chinese Communists.
subfiles.summary: The first item reports measures placing railway-car factories and repair capacity under unified control by the Railway Ministry to increase wartime production. A Mainichi editorial then discusses Nationalist pressure on the Yan'an Communists, unrest in Chinese regions, the Shaanxi–Gansu–Ningxia base, and the danger of renewed Kuomintang-Communist conflict; a short final item reports national bank deposits.

subfiles.title: Dōmei intercept on Japanese honors, Shanghai diplomacy, Thai territories, and Singapore salvage
subfiles.to: General radio audience; intercepted by U.S. monitoring personnel
subfiles.about: This transmission honors Japanese military and industrial personnel and reports administrative developments in Shanghai, Thailand, and occupied Singapore.
subfiles.summary: The broadcast praises Shigemasa Aoki, Tadao Odaira, Kinkichi Yamamoto, and civilian technicians for military courage or contributions to industrial production. It also reports enlargement of the Nanjing Foreign Ministry's Shanghai office, Thai planning for territorial transfers, and a detailed account of Japanese efforts to raise the scuttled King George V floating dry dock at Seletar.

subfiles.title: FCC forwarding letter transmitting additional Dōmei intercepts
subfiles.from: S. W. Norman, Acting Chief, FCC Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The FCC forwards additional copies of Dōmei press broadcasts intercepted from Japanese stations.
subfiles.summary: The confidential letter accompanies the preceding or attached radio-intercept copies and identifies FCC file 12718 and State Department file 894.76/145. It was sent by special messenger and subsequently filed by the Department of State.

subfiles.title: Dōmei dispatch on Turkish reaction to the American asylum note
subfiles.to: General radio audience; intercepted by the FCC
subfiles.about: An Istanbul dispatch reports Turkish press objections to an American note about denying asylum to Axis leaders.
subfiles.summary: The report says the Turkish government considered the American note compatible with international law and saw no need to reply. It nevertheless quotes Turkish newspapers attacking the note's threatening tone, its judgment of Axis leaders before the war's conclusion, and its alleged disregard for neutral sovereignty.

subfiles.title: Encrypted Dōmei transmission of 7 August 1943
subfiles.to: Unidentified recipient; intercepted by the FCC
subfiles.about: The sheets record messages numbered 38 through 45 almost entirely as encrypted numerical groups.
subfiles.summary: After the clear-language Istanbul item ends, a new transmission begins at 2130 on 7 August. Its message groups are preserved but not decoded in this section, so their subjects and intended recipient cannot be determined from the OCR.

subfiles.title: Dōmei intercept on Cebu, Saigon telecommunications, Yahagi's speech, and Berlin
subfiles.to: General radio audience; intercepted by the FCC
subfiles.about: A clear-language Dōmei broadcast reports regional news and reproduces Major General Nakao Yahagi's expansive wartime speech.
subfiles.summary: Short items cover restored bus service in Cebu, postponement of an Indian anti-Anglo-American rally, and an agreement permitting Japanese katakana telegrams between Saigon and Japanese-occupied areas. Yahagi depicts the war as Japanese self-defense and preparation for a sweeping offensive, while the final item lists senior German military and political leaders attending conferences at Hitler's headquarters.

subfiles.title: Encrypted Dōmei transmission beginning 7 August 1943
subfiles.to: Unidentified recipient; intercepted by the FCC
subfiles.about: A second long transmission is recorded as undeciphered numerical groups.
subfiles.summary: The coded traffic begins after the Berlin report on page 328 and continues through page 334. Although message numbers and separators are visible, the OCR supplies no deciphered prose from which to determine the subjects.

subfiles.title: Dōmei continuation and addendum to Yahagi's Greater East Asia speech
subfiles.to: General radio audience; intercepted by the FCC
subfiles.about: A fragmentary transmission adds material to Yahagi's speech and begins a Manila report before reception ends.
subfiles.summary: After a damaged notice of Philippine examination sites, the broadcast resumes Yahagi's claims that Japanese rule was winning native cooperation and turning East Asia's population and resources into fighting power. It praises Burmese and prospective Philippine independence, Wang Ching-wei's government, Sun Yat-sen's pan-Asianism, Germany's new European order, and the imperial doctrine of hakkō ichiu; a Manila item is cut off almost immediately.

subfiles.title: FCC forwarding letter transmitting additional Dōmei intercepts
subfiles.from: S. W. Norman, Acting Chief, FCC Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The FCC forwards another set of Dōmei press intercepts from Japanese stations.
subfiles.summary: This confidential special-messenger letter identifies FCC file 12718 and State Department file 894.76/146. It serves as the cover letter for the August broadcast intercepts that follow.

subfiles.title: Dōmei intercept on customary courts, Philippine agriculture, Sumatra, and a Thai delegation
subfiles.to: General radio audience; intercepted by the FCC
subfiles.about: A partly damaged transmission reports on customary courts, Japanese agricultural practices, Sumatra, and a Thai publicity delegation in Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: The opening fragment describes village, district, and provincial courts applying the customary law of an unidentified ethnic group. Hilarion Silayan praises Japanese cooperative harvesting and intensive farming, a Medan newspaper urges Sumatrans toward disciplined family-based leadership, and Pairot Jaiyanama's delegation calls on senior Manchukuo officials; the transmission ends with a Buenos Aires correction.

subfiles.title: French-language Dōmei intercept on Indochina, the Philippines, North China, and diplomacy
subfiles.to: General radio audience; intercepted by the FCC
subfiles.about: French-language reports cover French Indochina, a Thai visit to Manchukuo, Philippine cultural policy, Communist arrests, Burmese independence, and diplomatic movements.
subfiles.summary: The broadcast reports Jean Decoux's inspection of bombing damage, Masayuki Yokoyama's return to Hanoi, and Pairot Jaiyanama's calls on Manchukuo officials. Other items quote Jorge Vargas on Philippine cultural independence, report arrests of alleged Communist agents near Datong, exchange congratulatory messages between Chang Ching-hui and Tojo over Burmese independence, note the Japanese embassy's planned return from Kuybyshev to Moscow, and discuss Kiska and Shanghai price controls.

subfiles.title: Dōmei intercept on war relief, Thai students, Indonesian music, and machine tools
subfiles.to: General radio audience; intercepted by the FCC
subfiles.about: An English-language transmission reports charitable remittances, Thai-Japanese student exchanges, arrests in Mengjiang, musical propaganda in Indonesia, and Japanese machine tools.
subfiles.summary: Items describe funds sent from French Indochina to France, a meeting of Thai students with Japanese war-bereaved pupils in Toyama, and the arrest of alleged Communist agents around the Sanggan River. Ichirō Fujiyama praises Indonesian musical ability and Japanese-sponsored free concerts, while the final complete item claims major material and efficiency gains in newly designed Japanese machine tools.

subfiles.title: Fragmentary Dōmei item quoting Yūzō Isono on neutral-state rights
subfiles.to: General radio audience; intercepted by the FCC
subfiles.about: A damaged item begins Yūzō Isono's condemnation of American policy toward neutral states and Axis political refugees.
subfiles.summary: Only the opening lines of the transmission printed before reception ended. They identify Yūzō Isono and characterize the United States as deliberately trampling neutral rights, a subject reported more fully in the following intercept.

subfiles.title: Dōmei intercept on Philippine post offices, the Thai mission, neutral asylum, and W. W. Yen
subfiles.to: General radio audience; intercepted by the FCC
subfiles.about: A multipart broadcast reports Philippine postal expansion, Pairot Jaiyanama's tour, Communist arrests, Japanese criticism of Allied asylum policy, and W. W. Yen's business plans.
subfiles.summary: The opening item lists newly reopened Philippine post offices, followed by Pairot Jaiyanama's praise for Manchukuo's industrial development and Japanese home-front unity. Further reports repeat the arrest of alleged Communist agents near Datong and quote Yūzō Isono accusing Roosevelt and Churchill of violating neutral sovereignty by demanding denial of asylum to Axis leaders. The final, incomplete item says former ambassador W. W. Yen and other Shanghai financiers sought permission from Nanjing to establish an investment company.
